title: Priority TTL Orchestration and Client Backoff Guidance
content:
Goal:
Quick reference and decision guidance for orchestrating region-level evacuations that minimize client-visible errors while preserving throughput and ttl sanity. This doc is intentionally pragmatic — operator checklist + commands + telemetry guards + gotchas.

Summary of problem space and why TTL matters:
- DNS TTLs control how quickly traffic can be pulled off a region. Low TTLs = faster cutover but higher DNS query load and risk of oscillation. High TTLs = long tail of clients still hitting degraded region.
- Many customers and SDKs implement sticky egress (egress affinity) and aggressive client-side retries. Those behaviors interact with TTL change and can create transient overloads or request storms during shifts.
- We need a predictable, observable pattern to: 1) move traffic gradually 2) pre-warm warm-standby caches & KV caches 3) avoid client cascades due to misaligned backoff/retry policies.

High-level strategy (operator intent):
1) Prepare: ensure warm-standby is fully primed before shifting any significant weight. Run KV / embedding pre-seed if applicable.
2) Stage TTL adjustments: reduce effective DNS TTL at edge only after warm-standby ready, but not to < 30s unless absolutely necessary. Use staged TTLs per-region (e.g., 300s -> 120s -> 60s -> 30s) with telemetry windows between steps.
3) Shift capacity-weighted traffic with short windows and circuit-breaker thresholds. Prefer weighted routing at layer that understands KV affinity (if available).
4) Observe for client retry storm signals and pause shifts if observed.

Operator checklist (quick):
- [ ] Confirm warm-standby GPU pool health (GPU temp, free memory, KV cache entries, last model load). Command: kubectl -n dedicated get pods -l pool=warm-standby -o wide
- [ ] Prime KV cache: run preseed job (ops/kvcache-preseed --scope region-eu-west-1 --prefixes top-1000).
- [ ] Validate route table: curl -sS https://routing-api.internal/v1/routes?region=eu-west-1 | jq .weights
- [ ] Set DNS TTL stage 1: update dns-config service: PATCH /dns/config {"ttl_override":300} (or manual console change)
- [ ] Update monitoring window: start 5m high-resolution (10s) tracing for ingress/egress for the region being shifted.

Staged execution plan (detailed):
Phase A — Prime & validate (T-30m to T-5m)
- Verify warm-standby model binary checksum matches active region.
- Run small synthetic traffic smoke test (10 RPS) against warm-standby using test-client with identical headers/cookies to prod. Confirm latency P50/P95 within expected SLO.
- Confirm KV hit-rate >= 80% for standard prompts. If <80%, extend preseed or throttle shift.
- Verify autoscaler target counts and that cluster can scale to target throughput.

Phase B — Reduce TTL incrementally and observe (T-5m to T+15m)
Step 1: TTL -> 300s (if currently 600s)
- Wait 5m, check: 1) DNS query rate, 2) client error 5xx rates, 3) source-region CPU/GPU NVMM. If stable, proceed.
PromQL hints to run in Grafana:
- rate(dns_requests_total[1m]) by (region)
- sum(rate(http_requests_total{region=\"eu-west-1\",code=~\"5..\"}[1m]))
- avg_over_time(gpu_utilization{region=\"eu-west-1\"}[5m])

Step 2: TTL -> 120s
- Wait 5m, repeat checks. At each step, watch for: client retry amplification (sudden spike in identical request hashes), redis cache miss rate spike, or queue length growth in ingress buffers.

Phase C — Weighted traffic shift (after TTL low enough to allow real re-routing)
- Start with 10% weight to target region for 2 min. Monitor: latency delta per-verb, error rate by client-id, kvcache hit rate.
- Increase 10% every 2 min if all metrics stable. Pause on: error rate increase > 2x baseline or sudden 20% drop in cache hit-rate.

Client backoff and retry mitigations (common pain points):
- Many SDKs retry aggressively with short backoff (500ms). Coordinate with product/devx teams to release a temporary client-side advisory: increase base backoff to 1s and jitter enabled during active failover windows.
- For clients behind load balancers with TCP keepalives, connection pooling can cause long-tail hits to old region. Recommend clients use DNS TTL-aware pool refresh (e.g., close connections on TTL change event).

Telemetry signals that indicate a client-induced storm:
- Sudden increase in repeated identical request fingerprint counts in last 1m window. Example query: sum(rate(request_fingerprint_bucket{window=\"1m\"}[1m])) by (fingerprint)
- Surge in ingress 429s + 5xxs with matching user-agent patterns (language SDKs).
- Redis/kv cache miss ratio jumps and origin request rate grows.

Runbook abort and rollback criteria:
- Abort if 5xx error rate in target or source region > 3x baseline for >2 consecutive 1m buckets.
- Abort if GPU OOMs or model reload failures occur.
- Rollback steps: 
  1) Immediately set routing weights back to last known-good (e.g., 80/20 -> 100/0).
  2) Increase DNS TTL back to previous stable value in two steps (e.g., 60s -> 120s -> 300s) to give clients time to settle.
  3) Run remediation playbooks for caches and autoscaler.

Post-cutover validation checklist (after 100% shift or evacuation completed):
- Confirm 95th percentile latency at or below SLO for target region.
- Confirm no sustained error-rate delta > 1.5x baseline for 30m post cutover.
- Confirm billing/egress cost projection aligns with expected (avoid surprise egress delta).
- Create quick incident note in Slack and tag product and SDK teams with observed client behaviors.

Operational gotchas & lessons learned (from past incidents):
- Lowering TTL too early caused a DDOS-style DNS spike on our authoritative hosts — pre-warm secondary DNS capacity or stage internal DNS caches first.
- Some customers have home-grown SDKs that ignore TTL changes for minutes due to aggressive connection reuse; they should be on a compatibility doc.
- Warm-standby may appear healthy at binary level but still have empty KV caches — always preseed.
- Human communication matters: coordinate with comms to send a single advisory to engineering and support channels; multiple conflicting advisories have caused confusion during past shifts.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we standardize on a minimum observable TTL of 60s for all public regions? (Pros: faster cutover. Cons: higher DNS churn.) @product for policy decision.
- Can we implement an edge-side TTL override that only affects internal LB resolution, not public DNS? (Would allow faster operator changes without public churn.) @infra/edge
- Build a synthetic client that mirrors top-20 customers' retry behavior for better canarying. TODO: Evan to sketch.

Appendix: quick commands and sample curl checks
- Check route weights: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://routing-api.internal/v1/routes | jq .
- Hit warm-standby smoke endpoint: curl -H "X-Test-Client: canary" https://eu-west-1-warm-standby.redwood-internal/api/health
- Promote routing weight (example): POST https://routing-api.internal/v1/routes/shift {"from":"us-west-2","to":"eu-west-1","weight":10}

Notes to self (operator shorthand):
- If you see ingress HTTP/2 GOAWAYs during shift, likely connection churn from TTL change; consider slowing TTL stepdown.
- When in doubt: pause and wait 2x observation window. Fast is good, but oscillations kill user experience.
